cards.question: Describe the three fetal shunts and what they become postnatally.
cards.answer: Ductus venosus — bypasses part of the liver from umbilical vein to IVC; becomes ligamentum venosum. Foramen ovale — bypasses pulmonary circulation, RA → LA; becomes fossa ovalis (patent in 25 % of adults). Ductus arteriosus — bypasses lungs, pulmonary artery → aorta; becomes ligamentum arteriosum. The ductus venosus shunts umbilical venous blood past part of the liver into the IVC; the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus divert blood away from fetal pulmonary circulation.

cards.question: What triggers closure of the ductus arteriosus and how is it managed if it fails?
cards.answer: At birth: ↑PaO₂, ↓pulmonary vascular resistance, ↓circulating prostaglandins (placenta removed). Functional closure within 24 h, anatomical closure by 3 weeks. Persistent PDA in preterm infants is treated with indomethacin or ibuprofen (COX inhibitors reducing PGE₂). In duct-dependent congenital heart disease, prostaglandin E₁ infusion (alprostadil) is used to keep the duct OPEN until surgical repair.

cards.question: Why is fetal haemoglobin (HbF) advantageous?
cards.answer: Two α + two γ chains (vs α₂β₂ in HbA). γ binds 2,3-DPG poorly → left-shifted curve with P50 ~2.5 kPa (vs 3.5 kPa in adult). Higher O₂ affinity allows the fetus to extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta (where umbilical venous PO₂ is only 4 kPa). HbF declines from 80 % at birth to <2 % by 6 months.
